claims.claim: A crescent-shaped bread, the Kipfel ('Chipfen'), is attested in Vienna in the 13th century: Jans Enikel's Fürstenbuch describes Viennese bakers presenting it to Duke Leopold VI at Christmas 1227.

evidence.quote: Im 13. Jahrhundert sind „Chipfen“ im babenbergischen Wien bezeugt.
evidence.translation: In the 13th century 'Chipfen' are attested in Babenberg Vienna.
Earliest written mention for Vienna: Jans Enenkel's Fürstenbuch (13th century), Leopold VI's entry at Christmas 1227.

evidence.quote: the crescent-shaped roll that had existed in Austria since at least the thirteenth century

claims.limits: The chronicle text was not checked directly; it is a literary chronicle, not an administrative record. The recipe of the medieval roll is unknown. BMLUK's further remark that such pastry was baked 'from AD 1000' is unsourced and is NOT used.

claims.claim: Kipfel are mentioned in Viennese records in 1630, 1652 and 1670, i.e. before the 1683 siege.

evidence.translation: Later attestations: 'kipfen' in 1630 (records of the Vienna Medical Faculty), 1652, and 1670 (imperial privilege for the baker Adam Spiel).

claims.limits: Single source; original records not checked.

claims.claim: The croissant/kipfel was invented by Viennese bakers who heard Ottoman sappers tunnelling during the 1683 siege (variant: Buda, 1686) and baked a crescent to celebrate.

evidence.quote: doch ist die vor allem von Moritz Bermann ... verbreitete Entstehungsgeschichte historisch nicht haltbar.
evidence.translation: however, the origin story spread mainly by Moritz Bermann is historically untenable.

evidence.quote: croissants are said to have originated in Budapest in 1686
evidence.location: history section, attributed there to Larousse Gastronomique

evidence.quote: there are no contemporary sources for any of these stories

claims.limits: The two official Austrian sources disagree on one detail (BMLUK: the baker Peter Wendler died in 1680; Wien Geschichte Wiki: the Wendlers are documented as bakers 1683-1691), so that detail is not used. Both reject the legend.

claims.claim: Marie Antoinette introduced the kipfel/croissant to France after her marriage in 1770.

evidence.quote: Angeblich machte … Marie Antoinette … das Kipfel als „Croissant“ … populär.
evidence.translation: Allegedly Marie Antoinette made the kipfel popular as the 'croissant'.

evidence.quote: Chevallier also debunks the well-circulated myth of Marie Antoinette bringing the pastry with her from Austria.

claims.claim: August Zang, a former Austrian artillery officer from Vienna, opened a Viennese bakery (the Boulangerie Viennoise) in Paris around 1838-1839; a French writer mentions it in a letter of late 1839.

evidence.quote: In late 1839, the French writer Saint-Beuve wrote to a friend
had been opened by an Austrian artillery officer, August Zang.
who opened the Boulangerie Viennoise around 1839.

evidence.translation: Zang went to Paris to introduce Viennese baked goods there (no year given).

claims.limits: The exact opening year is disputed across accounts (1837-1839, one outlier 1840). The narration says 'around 1838 or 1839'. Nearly all accounts depend on one historian (Chevallier).

claims.claim: The Boulangerie Viennoise stood at 92 rue de Richelieu.
claims.limits: Only tertiary pointers give the address; not confirmed in a source that could be read. NOT used in narration, labels or signage.

claims.claim: Zang's bakery sold kipfel and Kaisersemmel, did very good business and was quickly imitated; French bakers' version of the kipfel came to be called the croissant.

evidence.quote: did an excellent business with Wiener Kipfeln and Kaisersemmeln
Soon French 'Viennese bakeries' opened, and made what the French called a 'crescent', or croissant.
French bakers created this roll as an imitation of the Austrian kipfel introduced by August Zang's Viennese Bakery.

claims.limits: All three sources are by the same author; the 1872 magazine quote is reproduced by him.

claims.claim: Zang (born Vienna 2 Aug 1807, died 4 Mar 1888) returned to Vienna and founded the newspaper Die Presse, whose first issue appeared on 3 July 1848; he became known as a publisher.

evidence.quote: Die epochemachende großformatige Zeitung "Die Presse" erschien erstmals am 3. Juli 1848.
evidence.translation: The epoch-making large-format newspaper 'Die Presse' first appeared on 3 July 1848.

evidence.quote: August Zang would go on to immense success, not in baking, but as a press magnate.

claims.claim: The pastry sense of the French word 'croissant' is first recorded in a dictionary in 1863 (Littré): a small bread or cake in the shape of a crescent.

evidence.quote: 1863 pâtiss. (Littré)
Petit pain ou petit gâteau qui a la forme d'un croissant.
evidence.translation: Small bread or small cake in the shape of a crescent.
evidence.location: 'Usage en français' quoting Littré (pointer; Littré's site returned 403)

claims.limits: Earlier non-dictionary uses are reported (1840 per Chevallier's glossary; 1850 and 1853 per Wikipedia footnotes) but were not verified, so the narration only cites the 1863 dictionary.

claims.claim: The early French croissant was a kipfel-style bread roll, not a laminated pastry; the flaky laminated version came later.

evidence.quote: Then recipes began to appear for a version made with laminated dough (a French method).
would have made a buttery roll based on an Austrian kipfel, not a flaky croissant
French bakers replaced the brioche dough of the kipferl with a yeast-leavened laminated dough.

claims.claim: When laminated croissants first appeared is debated: 'near the end of the 19th century' in one account; the recipes usually cited were printed in 1905-1906 (Colombié); earlier (1896, 1904) and later (Goy, 1915) candidates are also named.

evidence.quote: It was near the end of the 19th century that French bakers began incorporating thin and buttery laminated dough
was published in 1906, in Paris, in Colombié's Nouvelle Encyclopédie culinaire.

evidence.translation: Table of contents lists 'Scheibenbogen's 1896 recipe for laminated croissants' and 'Favrais' 1904 recipe for laminated Croissants' (titles only, body not read).

claims.limits: No primary cookbook was read. The narration gives a range and says the date is debated.

claims.claim: A modern croissant is made from laminated yeast dough (pâte levée feuilletée): dough is wrapped around butter, rolled and folded repeatedly into many thin layers (each letter fold triples them: 3, 9, 27), cut into triangles and rolled; in the oven water turns to steam and pushes the layers apart.

evidence.quote: a buttery, flaky viennoiserie made with a pâte levée feuilleté (layered yeast-leavened dough).
evidence.location: definition quoted from Le Cordon Bleu Ottawa

evidence.quote: the dough expands as water is converted to steam, thus increasing the pressure between each dough layer.
Croissant dough is typically laminated until 16–50 fat layers are obtained.
La vapeur produite en cours de cuisson va séparer les différentes couches du feuilletage.
evidence.translation: The steam produced during baking separates the layers of the lamination.

claims.limits: The 3-9-27 sequence is arithmetic for three letter folds and falls inside the cited 16-50 range; bakers vary the number and type of folds, which the narration says.

claims.claim: Industrial croissants (machine-made, frozen before baking) appeared in the 1970s; the French chain La Croissanterie opened its first shop in 1977.

evidence.quote: In the early 1970s, the first industrialized croissants steamrolled right over this careful process.
opened the first La Croissanterie in 1977
but most things that are meticulous about it can be industrialized.

claims.limits: 'Early 1970s' (TASTE) vs 'late 1970s' (Wikipedia) for frozen dough: the narration says 'in the 1970s'.

claims.claim: Burger King introduced the Croissan'wich breakfast sandwich in 1983.

evidence.quote: bringing the Croissan'wich to Burger King in 1983.

claims.limits: One outlier source gives 1985; the newspaper cited by Wikipedia (Houston Chronicle, 1996) was not read.

claims.claim: A large share of croissants sold in French bakeries are baked from industrial frozen dough; estimates differ widely (30-40 % as of 2008 in one account, over 80 % of bakery viennoiseries in another).
claims.limits: Both figures come from tertiary pointers citing press articles that were not read; they use different bases and dates. The narration gives no number.

claims.claim: Sara Lee launched frozen croissants in the United States in 1981.
claims.limits: Seen only in search-result summaries; no readable source. NOT used in narration.

claims.claim: At the Paris World's Fair (Exposition universelle) of 1867 the Viennese bakery was a great success.

evidence.quote: Auf der Pariser Weltausstellung von 1867 war die Wiener Bäckerei ein großer Erfolg.
evidence.translation: At the Paris World Exhibition of 1867 the Viennese bakery was a great success.

claims.limits: Single source; the narration attributes the statement to the register.

claims.claim: In French, 'croissant' means crescent (an object in the shape of a crescent, attested c. 1260).

evidence.quote: Ca 1260 « objet en forme de croissant »
evidence.translation: c. 1260, 'object in the shape of a crescent'

claims.claim: The kipfel may have begun as a monastery pastry baked for Easter.

evidence.quote: Vermutlich handelt es sich um ein traditionelles Klostergebäck, das wahrscheinlich zu Ostern gebacken wurde.
evidence.translation: Presumably it is a traditional monastery pastry that was probably baked at Easter.

claims.limits: The source itself presents this as a presumption; the narration says it is a guess.

claims.claim: In French, viennoiserie is the name for bakery goods other than bread made from fermented or semi-laminated dough, croissant included; the word derives from viennois (Viennese).

evidence.quote: Ensemble des produits de boulangerie autres que le pain, à base de pâte fermentée ou demi-feuilletée
evidence.translation: Bakery products other than bread, made from fermented or semi-laminated dough (croissant, brioche, pain au chocolat...).

evidence.quote: Mot issu de l'entrée VIENNOIS
evidence.translation: Word derived from the entry VIENNOIS (Viennese).

claims.limits: No first attestation date given; the CNRTL etymology page for this word is empty. Larousse (definition only) agrees and lists croissant. Narration says only that the word means Viennese things; it does not date the word.
